news-6c9c75b33fa93c42bb10ffd888f0295694d.summary:
Before sunrise on October 18, an astronaut on the International Space Station photographed a nearly cloudless stretch of the United States. Chicago and Detroit stood out among the lights, while smaller cities and the roads connecting them traced a web across the Midwest.

NASA’s account, published on November 4, explains why these views matter beyond their beauty. Differences in the brightness and colour of city lights can help researchers study urban growth, changes in lighting technology and the restoration of power after storms. The photograph captures an earlier event; the reporting is new.
news-6c9c75b33fa93c42bb10ffd888f0295694d.body:
The photograph was taken at 4:54 a.m. Central Daylight Time on October 18, 2026. Along with Chicago and Detroit, NASA identifies Indianapolis, Cincinnati and Louisville in the scene. A band of green and orange airglow appears near the horizon, with sunlight approaching from the right.

NASA describes astronaut photography as one way to understand how cities change. A broad view can make a city’s lighting look uniform, while closer images reveal differences between lighting types. Researchers use the agency’s astronaut-photography archive to examine those variations.

The article also describes NASA’s Black Marble satellite data, which track nighttime lighting over time. These records have been used to investigate changes associated with infrastructure, LED lighting and power outages. The source includes the original photographs and technical details; this account focuses on what the observations reveal.

news-cdc665ae512021ce9a601fcd46758015a7e.summary:
Canadian astronaut Joshua Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon worked outside the International Space Station on October 29, installing a roll-out solar array. A photograph released in NASA’s November 3 account shows Kutryk above the South Atlantic, with the station about 267 miles above Earth.

Their work also prepared for another spacewalk, scheduled for November 5, to install the eighth and final array. NASA says the eight arrays together will increase the station’s available power by up to 30 percent. That next installation was still planned when the report was published.
news-cdc665ae512021ce9a601fcd46758015a7e.body:
NASA’s account connects a photograph of Joshua Kutryk above Earth with the practical work of maintaining the space station. Kutryk, a Canadian Space Agency astronaut, and NASA’s Anil Menon installed a new roll-out solar array during their October 29, 2026 spacewalk.

The pair also completed preparation for their next outing. The report identifies November 5 as the planned date for installing the final array in a set of eight and gives the expected combined power increase as up to 30 percent. This short source does not establish that the later installation has happened. The original photograph is credited to the Canadian Space Agency.

news-b37cbeabc38bcc2e04231181f088bed5025.summary:
NASA announced an opportunity for students to speak with astronaut Anil Menon aboard the International Space Station and STEM creator Mark Rober on Earth. The Earth-to-space call was scheduled for November 4 at 11 a.m. Eastern time, with questions about life in microgravity and the work behind human spaceflight.

The programme is part of NASA’s National STEM Day activities. Its announcement also describes a new collaboration with the ClassCrunchLabs Foundation to widen access to science and engineering learning. The source describes the event’s plans and aims; it does not report attendance or outcomes.
news-b37cbeabc38bcc2e04231181f088bed5025.body:
NASA’s Office of STEM Engagement planned a live conversation linking classrooms with the International Space Station. Astronaut Anil Menon was scheduled to answer student questions and demonstrate how everyday tasks change in microgravity. Mark Rober, participating from California, was to discuss the curiosity and practical problem-solving behind his path from NASA engineer to STEM creator.

The November 3 announcement gives a start time of 11 a.m. Eastern on November 4 and directs viewers to NASA’s YouTube channel and Learn With NASA channels. It also announces a collaboration between NASA and the ClassCrunchLabs Foundation, combining agency educational resources with hands-on engineering content.

These are the organisers’ stated plans, rather than evidence of learning outcomes. The original announcement provides the event details and a reference page for NASA’s in-flight education calls.
